note: Questions from the CBSE Class XII Physics board exam 2025, Q.P. code 55/1/1, published by CBSE at cbse.gov.in. Q19 and Q32(a), which depend on figures, are left out; figures in other questions are described in words. Solutions are written for this portal and are not CBSE's official marking scheme.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A graph of the Coulomb force F between two point charges against 1/r² (r being their separation) is a straight line through the origin for each pair. For the pair (q₁, q₂) the line has a positive slope; for the pair (q₂, q₃) it has a negative slope that is less steep. If q₂ is positive and least in magnitude, then the magnitudes of q₁, q₂ and q₃ are such that
questions.solution: Slope = k q q′. The (q₁, q₂) line is steeper, so |q₁q₂| > |q₂q₃|, i.e. |q₁| > |q₃|. With q₂ the smallest: q₂ < q₃ < q₁. (The signs show q₁ is positive and q₃ negative.)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two wires P and Q are made of the same material. The wire Q has twice the diameter and half the length of wire P. If the resistance of wire P is R, the resistance of wire Q will be
questions.solution: R ∝ l/d². For Q: (1/2)/(2²) = 1/8 of R.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A voltage v = v₀ sin ωt applied to a circuit drives a current i = i₀ sin(ωt + φ) in the circuit. The average power consumed in the circuit over a cycle is
questions.solution: P = V_rms I_rms cos φ = (v₀i₀/2) cos φ.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A graph of photon energy against wavelength of electromagnetic waves falls steeply and then flattens. Point P is at a short wavelength (high energy), R at a middle wavelength and Q at a long wavelength (low energy). The points P, Q and R may correspond respectively to
questions.solution: E = hc/λ: shortest wavelength (P) is X-rays, middle (R) is UV and longest (Q) is microwaves. In the order P, Q, R: X-rays, microwaves, UV.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A beaker is filled with water (refractive index 4/3) up to a height H. A coin is placed at its bottom. The depth of the coin, when viewed along the near normal direction, will be
questions.solution: Apparent depth = real depth/μ = H/(4/3) = 3H/4.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.text: The stopping potential V₀ measured in a photoelectric experiment for a metal surface is plotted against frequency ν of the incident radiation. Let m be the slope of the straight line so obtained. Then the value of the charge of an electron is given by (h is Planck's constant)
questions.solution: eV₀ = hν − φ₀, so the slope is m = h/e and e = h/m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.text: Let λₑ, λₚ and λ_d be the wavelengths associated with an electron, a proton and a deuteron, all moving with the same speed. Then the correct relation between them is
questions.solution: λ = h/(mv); at the same speed, the lightest particle (electron) has the longest wavelength and the deuteron the shortest.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following describes the shape of the curve of binding energy per nucleon as a function of mass number A?
options: Rises steeply for light nuclei, has a broad maximum near A ≈ 56 and then decreases slowly
Rises steeply up to A ≈ 56 and then stays constant
A symmetric peak at A ≈ 80, falling equally on both sides
A sharp peak at A ≈ 80 followed by a steep fall
questions.solution: BE/A rises quickly for light nuclei, peaks at about 8.8 MeV near iron (A ≈ 56) and decreases slowly for heavy nuclei.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: When a p-n junction diode is forward biased
options: the barrier height and the depletion layer width both increase.
the barrier height increases and the depletion layer width decreases.
the barrier height and the depletion layer width both decrease.
the barrier height decreases and the depletion layer width increases.
questions.solution: Forward bias opposes the barrier potential, so both the barrier height and depletion width decrease.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Assertion (A): It is difficult to move a magnet into a coil of large number of turns when the circuit of the coil is closed.
Reason (R): The direction of induced current in a coil with its circuit closed, due to motion of a magnet, is such that it opposes the cause.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.solution: By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the motion of the magnet, so work must be done against it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Assertion (A): The deflection in a galvanometer is directly proportional to the current passing through it.
Reason (R): The coil of a galvanometer is suspended in a uniform radial magnetic field.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.solution: In a radial field the plane of the coil is always parallel to B, so the torque NIAB is proportional to I, and the deflection θ = (NAB/k)I.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Assertion (A): We cannot form a p-n junction diode by taking a slab of a p-type semiconductor and physically joining it to another slab of an n-type semiconductor.
Reason (R): In a p-type semiconductor nₑ ≫ nₕ while in an n-type semiconductor nₕ ≫ nₑ.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.solution: A physical join leaves gaps and surface roughness far larger than interatomic spacing, so A is true. R is false: in p-type, holes outnumber electrons (nₕ ≫ nₑ), and the reverse in n-type.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Assertion (A): The potential energy of an electron revolving in any stationary orbit in a hydrogen atom is positive.
Reason (R): The total energy of a charged particle is always positive.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.solution: The potential energy −ke²/r is negative, and the total energy of a bound electron is negative too. Both statements are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A battery of emf E and internal resistance r is connected to a rheostat. When a current of 2 A is drawn from the battery, the potential difference across the rheostat is 5 V. The potential difference becomes 4 V when a current of 4 A is drawn from the battery. Calculate the values of E and r.
questions.solution: V = E − Ir: 5 = E − 2r and 4 = E − 4r. Subtracting, 2r = 1, so r = 0.5 Ω and E = 6 V.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a diffraction experiment, the slit is illuminated by light of wavelength 600 nm. The first minimum of the pattern falls at θ = 30°. Calculate the width of the slit.
questions.solution: First minimum: a sin θ = λ, so a = 600 nm/0.5 = 1200 nm = 1.2 μm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, two light waves, each of intensity I₀, interfere at a point having a path difference λ/8 on the screen. Find the intensity at this point.
questions.solution: Phase difference φ = (2π/λ)(λ/8) = π/4. I = 4I₀cos²(φ/2) = 4I₀cos²(π/8) = 2I₀(1 + cos π/4) = 2I₀(1 + 1/√2) ≈ 3.41 I₀.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Prove that, in the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, the time period of revolution of an electron in the nth orbit is proportional to n³.
questions.solution: In the Bohr model rₙ = n²h²ε₀/(πme²) ∝ n² and vₙ = e²/(2ε₀nh) ∝ 1/n. So T = 2πrₙ/vₙ ∝ n²/(1/n) = n³.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A p-type Si semiconductor is made by doping an average of one dopant atom per 5 × 10⁷ silicon atoms. If the number density of silicon atoms in the specimen is 5 × 10²⁸ atoms m⁻³, find the number of holes created per cubic centimetre in the specimen due to doping. Also give one example of such dopants.
questions.solution: Dopant density = 5 × 10²⁸/(5 × 10⁷) = 10²¹ m⁻³; each creates one hole, so holes = 10²¹ m⁻³ = 10¹⁵ cm⁻³. Example: boron (or another trivalent atom such as Al, Ga, In).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two batteries of emfs 3 V and 6 V and internal resistances 0.2 Ω and 0.4 Ω are connected in parallel. This combination is connected to a 4 Ω resistor. Find : (i) the equivalent emf of the combination (ii) the equivalent internal resistance of the combination (iii) the current drawn from the combination.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) A conductor of length l is connected across an ideal cell of emf E. Keeping the cell connected, the length of the conductor is increased to 2l by gradually stretching it. If R and R′ are the initial and final values of resistance and v_d and v_d′ are the initial and final values of drift velocity, find the relation between (1) R′ and R and (2) v_d′ and v_d.
(ii) When electrons drift in a conductor from lower to higher potential, does it mean that all the 'free electrons' of the conductor are moving in the same direction?
questions.solution: (i) Volume is constant, so doubling the length halves the area: R′ = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4R. The field E/l halves and v_d = eEτ/(ml), so v_d′ = v_d/2. (ii) No. Free electrons move randomly in all directions; only their average (drift) motion is from lower to higher potential.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Using the Biot-Savart law, derive the expression for the magnetic field B due to a circular current carrying loop at a point on its axis and hence at its centre.
questions.solution: For a loop of radius R carrying current I, an element dl at distance r = √(R² + x²) from axial point P gives dB = μ₀I dl/(4πr²) perpendicular to r. The components perpendicular to the axis cancel in pairs; the axial components add: B = ∮ (μ₀I dl/(4πr²))(R/r) = μ₀IR²/(2(R² + x²)^(3/2)), along the axis. At the centre (x = 0): B = μ₀I/(2R).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(a) Show that the energy required to build up the current I in a coil of inductance L is ½LI².
(b) Considering the case of the magnetic field produced by an air-filled current carrying solenoid, show that the magnetic energy density of a magnetic field B is B²/(2μ₀).
questions.solution: (a) The back emf is L dI/dt, so the work done in time dt is dW = (L dI/dt) I dt = LI dI. Integrating from 0 to I: W = ½LI². (b) For a solenoid, L = μ₀n²Al and B = μ₀nI. U = ½LI² = ½μ₀n²AlI² = (B²/(2μ₀))Al. Dividing by the volume Al, energy density = B²/(2μ₀).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(a) A parallel plate capacitor is charged by an ac source. Show that the sum of the conduction current (I_c) and the displacement current (I_d) has the same value at all points of the circuit.
(b) In case (a) above, is Kirchhoff's first rule (junction rule) valid at each plate of the capacitor? Explain.
questions.solution: (a) In the wires there is only conduction current I_c = dq/dt. Between the plates the flux is Φ_E = q/ε₀, so I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = dq/dt = I_c. So I_c + I_d is the same everywhere: conduction current in the wires, displacement current in the gap. (b) Yes, provided the displacement current is counted: the conduction current reaching a plate equals the displacement current leaving it into the gap.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.text:
Answer the following giving reason :
(a) All the photoelectrons do not eject with the same kinetic energy when monochromatic light is incident on a metal surface.
(b) The saturation current in case (a) is different for different intensity.
(c) If one goes on increasing the wavelength of light incident on a metal surface, keeping its intensity constant, emission of photoelectrons stops at a certain wavelength for this metal.
questions.solution: (a) Electrons come from different depths and lose different amounts of energy in collisions before escaping; only surface electrons leave with the maximum kinetic energy. (b) The number of photoelectrons emitted per second is proportional to the number of incident photons, i.e. to intensity, so the saturation current depends on intensity. (c) Photon energy hc/λ decreases as λ increases; beyond the threshold wavelength it is less than the work function and no electron can be emitted.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(a) Define 'Mass defect' and 'Binding energy' of a nucleus. Describe the 'Fission process' on the basis of binding energy per nucleon.
(b) A deuteron contains a proton and a neutron and has a mass of 2.013553 u. Calculate the mass defect for it in u and its energy equivalence in MeV. (mₚ = 1.007277 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²)
questions.solution: (a) Mass defect: the difference between the total mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus. Binding energy: the energy equivalent of the mass defect (Δm c²), the energy needed to separate the nucleus into its nucleons. In fission a heavy nucleus (BE/A ≈ 7.6 MeV) splits into two middle-weight nuclei with higher BE/A (≈ 8.5 MeV); the increase in total binding energy is released. (b) Δm = 1.007277 + 1.008665 − 2.013553 = 0.002389 u; energy = 0.002389 × 931.5 ≈ 2.23 MeV.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(a) Draw a circuit arrangement for studying the V-I characteristics of a p-n junction diode.
(b) Show the shape of the characteristics of a diode.
(c) Mention two pieces of information that you can get from these characteristics.
questions.solution: (a) A battery with a rheostat (potential divider) connected across the diode through a milliammeter in series, with a voltmeter across the diode; the battery is reversed (and a microammeter used) for reverse bias. (b) Forward bias: current is negligible until the threshold (knee) voltage (≈ 0.7 V for Si), then rises steeply. Reverse bias: a very small, nearly constant current until breakdown voltage, where it rises sharply. (c) The threshold (knee) voltage, the dynamic resistance (ΔV/ΔI), the reverse breakdown voltage, and that the diode conducts mainly in one direction (rectification).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
A circuit consisting of a capacitor C, a resistor of resistance R and an ideal battery of emf V is known as an RC series circuit. Key S₁ connects the battery into the loop; key S₂ connects the capacitor and resistor in a loop without the battery. As soon as the circuit is completed by closing key S₁ (keeping S₂ open), charge begins to flow between the capacitor plates and the battery terminals. The charge on the capacitor increases and so does the potential difference V_c (= q/C) across it. When this equals the battery's potential difference, the capacitor is fully charged (Q = VC). During charging, q = Q[1 − e^(−t/RC)]. The charging current can be obtained by differentiating it, using d/dx (e^(mx)) = m e^(mx). Consider the case when R = 20 kΩ, C = 500 μF and V = 10 V.

The final charge on the capacitor, when key S₁ is closed and S₂ is open, is
questions.solution: Q = CV = 500 μF × 10 V = 5 mC.

questions.text:

Key S₁ connects the battery into the loop; key S₂ connects the capacitor and resistor in a loop without the battery. As soon as the circuit is completed by closing key S₁ (keeping S₂ open), charge begins to flow between the capacitor plates and the battery terminals. The charge on the capacitor increases and so does the potential difference V_c (= q/C) across it. When this equals the battery's potential difference, the capacitor is fully charged (Q = VC). During charging, q = Q[1 − e^(−t/RC)]. The charging current can be obtained by differentiating it, using d/dx (e^(mx)) = m e^(mx). Consider the case when R = 20 kΩ, C = 500 μF and V = 10 V.

For sufficient time the key S₁ is closed and S₂ is open. Now key S₂ is closed and S₁ is open. What is the final charge on the capacitor?
questions.solution: With the battery removed, the capacitor discharges completely through R.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which is spherical. Applying the formula for image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, one can obtain the 'lens maker formula' and then the 'lens formula'. A lens has two foci, called the 'first focal point' and the 'second focal point', one on each side. In an experiment, a glass plate with a black vertical arrow pointing up and a horizontal thick line with a ball at its right end is illuminated in a light box, and a convex lens forms its real image on a screen.

Which of the following correctly represents the image formed on the screen?
options: Arrow pointing up, ball at the right end
Arrow pointing up, ball at the left end
Arrow pointing down, ball at the left end
Arrow pointing down, ball at the right end
questions.solution: A real image formed by a convex lens is inverted both up-down and left-right.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which is spherical. Applying the formula for image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, one can obtain the 'lens maker formula' and then the 'lens formula'. A lens has two foci, called the 'first focal point' and the 'second focal point', one on each side. In an experiment, a glass plate with a black vertical arrow pointing up and a horizontal thick line with a ball at its right end is illuminated in a light box, and a convex lens forms its real image on a screen.

Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: For a convex mirror magnification is always negative.
For all virtual images formed by a mirror magnification is positive.
For a concave lens magnification is always positive.
For real and inverted images, magnification is always negative.
questions.solution: A convex mirror always forms virtual, erect images, so its magnification is positive.

A convex lens of focal length f is cut into two equal parts perpendicular to the principal axis. The focal length of each part will be
questions.solution: Each half is plano-convex with one curved surface, so its power halves and its focal length becomes 2f.

A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which is spherical. Applying the formula for image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, one can obtain the 'lens maker formula' and then the 'lens formula'. In an experiment, a glass plate with a black vertical arrow pointing up and a horizontal thick line with a ball at its right end is illuminated in a light box, and a convex lens forms its real image on a screen.

The distance of an object from the first focal point of a biconvex lens is X₁ and the distance of the image from the second focal point is X₂. The focal length of the lens is
questions.solution: Newton's formula: X₁X₂ = f², so f = √(X₁X₂).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) Two point charges 5 μC and −1 μC are placed at points (−3 cm, 0, 0) and (3 cm, 0, 0) respectively. An external electric field E = (A/r²) r̂, where A = 3 × 10⁵ V m, is switched on in the region. Calculate the change in electrostatic energy of the system due to the electric field.
(ii) A system of two conductors is placed in air and they have net charges of +80 μC and −80 μC, which causes a potential difference of 16 V between them. (1) Find the capacitance of the system. (2) If the air between the conductors is replaced by a dielectric medium of dielectric constant 3, what will be the potential difference between the two conductors? (3) If the charges on the two conductors are changed to +160 μC and −160 μC, will the capacitance of the system change? Give reason for your answer.
questions.solution: (i) The field E = A/r² r̂ has potential V = A/r. Both charges are at r = 0.03 m, where V = 3 × 10⁵/0.03 = 10⁷ V. Energy in the external field = (q₁ + q₂)V = (5 − 1) × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁷ = 40 J. (ii) (1) C = Q/V = 80 μC/16 V = 5 μF. (2) C becomes 15 μF, so V = 80/15 ≈ 5.3 V. (3) No; capacitance depends only on the size, shape and separation of the conductors and the medium, not on the charge (V doubles to 32 V).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) Consider three metal spherical shells A, B and C, each of radius R. Each shell has a concentric metal ball of radius R/10. The shells A, B and C are given charges +6q, −4q and 14q respectively. Their inner metal balls are given charges −2q, +8q and −10q respectively. Compare the magnitudes of the electric fields due to shells A, B and C at a distance 3R from their centres.
(ii) A charge −6 μC is placed at the centre B of a semicircle of radius 5 cm, with C and A the ends of its diameter. An equal and opposite charge is placed at point D on the line CA extended beyond C, at a distance of 10 cm from B. A charge +5 μC is moved from point C to point A along the circumference. Calculate the work done on the charge.
questions.solution: (i) At 3R the field depends only on the total charge enclosed: A: 6q − 2q = 4q; B: −4q + 8q = 4q; C: 14q − 10q = 4q. The fields are equal, 1 : 1 : 1. (ii) DC = 5 cm, DA = 15 cm, BC = BA = 5 cm. V_C = k(−6/0.05 + 6/0.05) × 10⁻⁶ = 0. V_A = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁶ (−6/0.05 + 6/0.15) = −7.2 × 10⁵ V. Work done by the external agent = q(V_A − V_C) = 5 × 10⁻⁶ × (−7.2 × 10⁵) = −3.6 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) Derive an expression for the torque acting on a rectangular current loop suspended in a uniform magnetic field.
(ii) A charged particle is moving in a circular path with velocity V in a uniform magnetic field B. It is made to pass through a sheet of lead and as a consequence, it loses one half of its kinetic energy without change in its direction. How will (1) the radius of its path (2) its time period of revolution change?
questions.solution: (i) For a loop of sides a, b carrying current I with its normal at angle θ to B: the forces on the sides of length a are IaB each, equal and opposite, separated by b sin θ, forming a couple. τ = IaB × b sin θ = IAB sin θ; for N turns τ = NIAB sin θ, i.e. τ = m × B with m = NIA. (ii) Half the KE means v becomes v/√2. (1) r = mv/(qB), so r becomes r/√2. (2) T = 2πm/(qB) does not depend on v, so it is unchanged.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) (1) What are coherent sources? Why are they necessary for observing a sustained interference pattern? (2) Lights from two independent sources are not coherent. Explain.
(ii) Two slits 0.1 mm apart are arranged 1.20 m from a screen. Light of wavelength 600 nm from a distant source is incident on the slits. (1) How far apart will adjacent bright interference fringes be on the screen? (2) Find the angular width (in degree) of the first bright fringe.
questions.solution: (i) (1) Sources that emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference. A constant phase difference keeps the positions of maxima and minima fixed, so the pattern is sustained. (2) In independent sources, atoms emit randomly with phases changing about every 10⁻⁸ s, so the phase difference is not constant. (ii) (1) β = λD/d = 600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.2/10⁻⁴ = 7.2 mm. (2) Angular width = λ/d = 6 × 10⁻³ rad ≈ 0.34°.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) Define a wavefront. An incident plane wave falls on a convex lens and gets refracted through it. Draw a diagram to show the incident and refracted wavefront.
(ii) A beam of light coming from a distant source is refracted by a spherical glass ball (refractive index 1.5) of radius 15 cm. Draw the ray diagram and obtain the position of the final image formed.
questions.solution: (i) A wavefront is the locus of points oscillating in the same phase. A plane wavefront passing through a convex lens becomes a spherical wavefront converging to the focus (the middle is delayed more, as the lens is thickest there). (ii) First surface: 1.5/v − 1/∞ = (1.5 − 1)/15, so v = 45 cm from the first surface, i.e. 15 cm beyond the second surface (a virtual object). Second surface: u = +15 cm, R = −15 cm: 1/v − 1.5/15 = (1 − 1.5)/(−15), so 1/v = 1/30 + 1/10 and v = 7.5 cm. The final image is 7.5 cm beyond the ball (22.5 cm from its centre).
